q-343194.name: Question 1
q-343194.problem:
![](/home/jake/Developer/Course_Academy/reference/mathacademy/capture/foundations/14187947/assets/996768e4b1ce8ae57bcf3cce61059f8349c307ea9f05c9c1f51831ff6fd8ae68.png)

A rectangular loaf of rising bread dough is squeezed between two rigid side panels that keep its width fixed. The length of the loaf is decreasing by $20\,\text{mm}\text{/s},$ while the $60\,\text{mm}$ width does not change. If the volume of the loaf is constant, how fast is its height changing when its dimensions are $100\,\text{mm}$ in length and $30\,\text{mm}$ in height?

The height is increasing at a rate of
{{field-1}}
$\text{mm}/\text{s}.$
q-343194.worked_solution:
Let $x,y,z$ be the dimensions of the solid, and let $V$ be its volume. We are given that 

$$
\begin{aligned}x & =100\,\text{mm}, \\ y & =60\,\text{mm}, \\ z & =30\,\text{mm}.\end{aligned}
$$

Also, we know that

$$
\begin{aligned}\frac{\text{d}x}{\text{d}t} & =-20\,\text{mm}\text{/s}, \\ \frac{\text{d}V}{\text{d}t} & =0\,{\text{mm}}^{3}\text{/s}.\end{aligned}
$$

We would like to find $\frac{\text{d}z}{\text{d}t}$ when $x=100\,\text{mm},$ $y=60\,\text{mm}$ and $z=30\,\text{mm}.$

We start with the formula for the volume of the rectangular prism:

$$
V=xyz
$$

Since $y$ is not changing and $y=60,$ we get

$$
V=60xz.
$$

Now, we differentiate with respect to time using the chain rule, and we get

$$
\begin{aligned}\frac{\text{d}V}{\text{d}t} & =\frac{\text{d}}{\text{d}t}(60xz) \\ \frac{\text{d}V}{\text{d}t} & =60x(\frac{\text{d}z}{\text{d}t})+60z(\frac{\text{d}x}{\text{d}t}).\end{aligned}
$$

We can now plug in the known values into the above expression. This gives

$$
\begin{aligned}0 & =60(100)(\frac{\text{d}z}{\text{d}t})+60(30)(-20) \\ 0 & =6000(\frac{\text{d}z}{\text{d}t})-36\,000 \\ 36\,000 & =6000(\frac{\text{d}z}{\text{d}t}) \\ \frac{\text{d}z}{\text{d}t} & =6\,\text{mm}\text{/s}.\end{aligned}
$$

Therefore, the height of the solid is increasing at a rate of $6\,\text{mm}/\text{s}$ at the moment when $x=100\,\text{mm},$ $y=60\,\text{mm}$ and $z=30\,\text{mm}.$

q-2795.name: Question 2
q-2795.problem:
![](/home/jake/Developer/Course_Academy/reference/mathacademy/capture/foundations/14187947/assets/52448daf1f9aea06b4ab4713756080ddb3ab465b4fae8f92b65a54c251a81d5e.png)

The length of a rectangular prism is decreasing by $8\,\text{cm}\text{/min}$ and its height increasing at a rate of $1\,\text{cm/min}.$ If the volume of the rectangular prism is decreasing at a rate of $50\,{\text{cm}}^{3}\text{/min},$  how fast is its width changing when its dimensions are $10\,\text{cm}$ in length, $15\,\text{cm}$ in width and $5\,\text{cm}$ in height?
q-2795.worked_solution:
Let $x,y,z$ be the dimensions of the solid, and let $V$ be its volume. We are given that 

$$
\begin{aligned}x & =10\text{ cm}, \\ y & =5\text{ cm}, \\ z & =15\text{ cm}.\end{aligned}
$$

Also, we know that

$$
\begin{aligned}\frac{\text{d}x}{\text{d}t} & =-8\text{ cm}\text{/min}, \\ \frac{\text{d}y}{\text{d}t} & =1\text{ cm}\text{/min}, \\ \frac{\text{d}V}{\text{d}t} & =-50{\text{ cm}}^{3}\text{/min}.\end{aligned}
$$

We would like to find $\frac{\text{d}z}{\text{d}t}$ when $x=10\,\text{cm},$ $y=5\,\text{cm},$ and $z=15\,\text{cm}.$

We start with the formula for the volume of the rectangular prism:

$$
V=xyz
$$

Now, we differentiate with respect to time using the chain rule, and we get

$$
\begin{aligned}\frac{\text{d}V}{\text{d}t} & =\frac{\text{d}}{\text{d}t}(x\cdot y\cdot z) \\ \frac{\text{d}V}{\text{d}t} & =xy(\frac{\text{d}z}{\text{d}t})+xz(\frac{\text{d}y}{\text{d}t})+yz(\frac{\text{d}x}{\text{d}t})\end{aligned}
$$

We can now plug in the known values into the above expression. This gives

$$
\begin{aligned}-50 & =(10)(5)(\frac{\text{d}z}{\text{d}t})+(10)(15)(1)+(15)(5)(-8) \\ \frac{\text{d}z}{\text{d}t} & =8\text{ cm}\text{/min}.\end{aligned}
$$

Therefore, the width of the solid is increasing at a rate of $8\,\text{cm}/\text{min}$ at the moment when $x=10\,\text{cm},$ $y=5\,\text{cm},$ and $z=15\,\text{cm}.$

q-2795.html:
Question 2
?

The length of a rectangular prism is decreasing by 8cm/min and its height increasing at a rate of 1cm/min. If the volume of the rectangular prism is decreasing at a rate of 50cm3/min, how fast is its width changing when its dimensions are 10cm in length, 15cm in width and 5cm in height?

a
12cm/min
b
7cm/min
c
8cm/min
d
4cm/min
e
9cm/min
Submit
Incorrect
EXPLANATION

Let x,y,z be the dimensions of the solid, and let V be its volume. We are given that x=10 cm,y=5 cm,z=15 cm.

Also, we know that

dxdt=−8 cm/min,dydt=1 cm/min,dVdt=−50 cm3/min.

We would like to find dzdt when x=10cm, y=5cm, and z=15cm.

We start with the formula for the volume of the rectangular prism: V=xyz

Now, we differentiate with respect to time using the chain rule, and we get

dVdt=ddt(x⋅y⋅z)dVdt=xy(dzdt)+xz(dydt)+yz(dxdt)

We can now plug in the known values into the above expression. This gives −50=(10)(5)(dzdt)+(10)(15)(1)+(15)(5)(−8)dzdt=8 cm/min.

Therefore, the width of the solid is increasing at a rate of 8cm/min at the moment when x=10cm, y=5cm, and z=15cm.

Jennie fills an aquarium, in the shape of a rectangular prism that is $50\,\text{cm}$ long and $25\,\text{cm}$ wide, with water from a tap. What is the rate of change of the water level if the volume is increasing at a rate of $250\,{\text{cm}}^{3}/\text{h}?$

The water level is increasing at a rate of
{{field-1}}
$\text{cm}/\text{h}.$
q-343180.worked_solution:
Let $x,y,z$ be the dimensions of the rectangular prism, let $V$ be its volume. We are given that 

$$
\begin{aligned}x & =50\,\text{cm}, \\ y & =25\,\text{cm}.\end{aligned}
$$

Also, we know that

$$
\frac{\text{d}V}{\text{d}t}=250\,{\text{cm}}^{3}/\text{h}.
$$

We would like to find $\frac{\text{d}z}{\text{d}t}$ when $x=50\,\text{cm}$ and $y=25\,\text{cm}.$

We start with the formula for the volume of the rectangular prism:

$$
V=xyz
$$

Substituting the known values, we get

$$
V=(50)(25)z=1250z.
$$

Now, we differentiate with respect to time using the chain rule, and we get

$$
\begin{aligned}\frac{\text{d}V}{\text{d}t} & =\frac{\text{d}}{\text{d}t}(1250z) \\ \frac{\text{d}V}{\text{d}t} & =1250(\frac{\text{d}z}{\text{d}t}).\end{aligned}
$$

We can now plug in the known value into the above expression. This gives

$$
\begin{aligned}250 & =1250(\frac{\text{d}z}{\text{d}t}) \\ \frac{\text{d}z}{\text{d}t} & =0.2\,\text{cm}\text{/h}.\end{aligned}
$$

Therefore, the water level is increasing at a rate of $0.2\,\text{cm}/\text{h}.$

q-116080.name: Question 4
q-116080.problem:
![](/home/jake/Developer/Course_Academy/reference/mathacademy/capture/foundations/14187947/assets/e11ec3379c969bbc8499f36978f3a39efe1342ee6563569949dbcb61611ab5f4.png)

A cube of ice is melting uniformly at a rate of $204\,{\text{cm}}^{3}\text{/min},$ where $x$ is the length of its edge. How fast is each edge of the ice block decreasing when the volume of the cube is $216\,{\text{cm}}^{3}?$
q-116080.worked_solution:
Let $V$ be the volume of the ice cube. We are given that 

$$
\begin{aligned}\frac{\text{d}V}{\text{d}t}=-204\,{\text{cm}}^{3}/\text{min}.\end{aligned}
$$

We would like to find $\frac{\text{d}x}{\text{d}t}$ when $V=216\,{\text{cm}}^{3}.$

  We start with the formula for the volume of the cube:
  

$$
V={x}^{3}
$$

Now, we differentiate with respect to time using the chain rule, and we get

$$
\begin{aligned}\frac{\text{d}}{\text{d}t}(V) & =\frac{\text{d}}{\text{d}t}({x}^{3}) \\ \frac{\text{d}V}{\text{d}t} & =3{x}^{2}\cdot \frac{\text{d}x}{\text{d}t}.\end{aligned}
$$

Before we plug in the known values, we need to find the value of $x$ when $V=216\,{\text{cm}}^{3}.$ We get

$$
\begin{aligned}V & ={x}^{3} \\ 216 & ={x}^{3} \\ x & =6.\end{aligned}
$$

We can now plug $x=6$ and $\frac{\text{d}V}{\text{d}t}=-204$ into the expression for $\frac{\text{d}x}{\text{d}t}.$ This gives

$$
\begin{aligned}\frac{\text{d}V}{\text{d}t} & =3{x}^{2}\cdot \frac{\text{d}x}{\text{d}t} \\ -204 & =3(6)^{2}\cdot \frac{\text{d}x}{\text{d}t} \\ \frac{\text{d}x}{\text{d}t} & =-\frac{17}{9}.\end{aligned}
$$

Therefore, the sides of the cube are decreasing at a rate of $\frac{17}{9}\,\text{cm}/\text{min}$ at the moment when $x=6\,\text{cm}.$

A cube of ice is melting uniformly at a rate of 204cm3/min, where x is the length of its edge. How fast is each edge of the ice block decreasing when the volume of the cube is 216cm3?

a
119cm/min
b
179cm/min
c
173cm/min
d
617cm/min
e
176cm/min

EXPLANATION

Let V be the volume of the ice cube. We are given that dVdt=−204cm3/min.

We would like to find dxdt when V=216cm3.

We start with the formula for the volume of the cube: V=x3

Now, we differentiate with respect to time using the chain rule, and we get

ddt(V)=ddt(x3)dVdt=3x2⋅dxdt.

Before we plug in the known values, we need to find the value of x when V=216cm3. We get

V=x3216=x3x=6.

We can now plug x=6 and dVdt=−204 into the expression for dxdt. This gives

dVdt=3x2⋅dxdt−204=3(6)2⋅dxdtdxdt=−179.

Therefore, the sides of the cube are decreasing at a rate of 179cm/min at the moment when x=6cm.

$\text{feet}/\text{min}.$
q-314513.worked_solution:
Let $x,y,z$ be the dimensions of the solid, and let $V$ be its volume. We are given that 

$$
\begin{aligned}x & =5\,\text{feet}, \\ y & =3\,\text{feet}, \\ z & =2\,\text{feet}.\end{aligned}
$$

Also, we know that

$$
\begin{aligned}\frac{\text{d}x}{\text{d}t} & =-1.5\,\text{feet}\text{/min}, \\ \frac{\text{d}z}{\text{d}t} & =1\,\text{feet}\text{/min}, \\ \frac{\text{d}V}{\text{d}t} & =-9\,{\text{feet}}^{3}\text{/min}.\end{aligned}
$$

We would like to find $\frac{\text{d}y}{\text{d}t}$ when $x=5\,\text{feet},$ $y=3\,\text{feet},$ and $z=2\,\text{feet}.$

We start with the formula for the volume of the rectangular prism:

$$
V=xyz
$$

Now, we differentiate with respect to time using the chain rule, and we get

$$
\begin{aligned}\frac{\text{d}V}{\text{d}t} & =\frac{\text{d}}{\text{d}t}(x\cdot y\cdot z) \\ \frac{\text{d}V}{\text{d}t} & =xy(\frac{\text{d}z}{\text{d}t})+xz(\frac{\text{d}y}{\text{d}t})+yz(\frac{\text{d}x}{\text{d}t}).\end{aligned}
$$

We can now plug in the known values into the above expression. This gives

$$
\begin{aligned}-9 & =(5)(3)(1)+(5)(2)(\frac{\text{d}y}{\text{d}t})+(2)(3)(-1.5) \\ -9 & =15+10\cdot (\frac{\text{d}y}{\text{d}t})-9 \\ \frac{\text{d}y}{\text{d}t} & =-1.5.\end{aligned}
$$

Therefore, the width of the solid is decreasing at a rate of $1.5\,\text{feet}/\text{min}$ at the moment when $x=5\,\text{feet},$ $y=2\,\text{feet},$ and $z=3\,\text{feet}.$

If the surface area of a cube is increasing at a rate of $144{\text{ cm}}^{2}\text{/s},$ at what rate are the edges changing when each edge is $4\text{ cm}?$ Assume that each edge is increasing at the same rate.
q-116519.worked_solution:
Let $x$ be the side of the cube, let $S$ be its surface area, and let $V$ be its volume. All of the variables change with time. In particular, we are given that 

$$
\begin{aligned}\frac{\text{d}S}{\text{d}t}=144\,{\text{cm}}^{2}/\text{s}.\end{aligned}
$$

We would like to find $\frac{\text{d}x}{\text{d}t}$ when $x=4\,\text{cm}.$

We want to find the rate of change of $x$ knowing the rate of change of $S.$ So, we start with the formula for the surface area of the cube:

$$
S=6{x}^{2}
$$

Now, we differentiate with respect to time using the chain rule, and we get

$$
\begin{aligned}\frac{\text{d}}{\text{d}t}(S) & =\frac{\text{d}}{\text{d}t}(6{x}^{2}) \\ \frac{\text{d}S}{\text{d}t} & =12x\frac{\text{d}x}{\text{d}t}.\end{aligned}
$$

We can now plug in the known values into the above expression. This gives

$$
\begin{aligned}\frac{\text{d}S}{\text{d}t} & =12x\frac{\text{d}x}{\text{d}t} \\ 144 & =12(4)\frac{\text{d}x}{\text{d}t} \\ \frac{\text{d}x}{\text{d}t} & =3.\end{aligned}
$$

Therefore, the edges are changing at a rate of $3\,\text{cm}/\text{s}.$

Question 10
?

The length of a rectangular prism is decreasing at a rate of 3cm/min, the width is increasing at a rate of 5cm/min, and the 5cm height does not change. How fast is the surface area of the rectangular prism decreasing when its dimensions are 3cm in length and 10cm in width?

a
 10 cm2/min
b
 12 cm2/min
c
 20 cm2/min
d
 15 cm2/min
e
 5 cm2/min
Submit
Correct
EXPLANATION

Let x,y,z be the dimensions of the solid, and let V be its volume. We are given that x=3cm,y=10cm,z=5cm,dxdt=−3cm/min,dydt=5cm/min.

We would like to find dSdt.

We want to find the rate of change of S knowing the rate of change of x and y. So, we start with the formula for the surface area of the rectangular prism: S=2xz+2xy+2yz

Since z=5cm is not changing, we get S=10x+2xy+10y.

Now, we differentiate with respect to time using the chain rule, and we get

dSdt=ddt(10x+2xy+10y)dSdt=(2x+10)(dydt)+(10+2y)(dxdt).

We can now plug in the known values into the above expression. This gives dSdt=(2⋅3+10)(5)+(10+2⋅10)(−3)=80−90=−10cm2/min.

Therefore, the surface area of the rectangular prism is decreasing at a rate of 10cm2/min.

The edges of a cube decrease at a rate of $9\text{ cm/s}.$ At what rate is the volume decreasing when the length of each edge is $40\text{ cm}?$
q-30081.worked_solution:
Let $x$ be the side length of the cube and let $V$ be its volume. We are given that 

$$
\begin{aligned}\frac{\text{d}x}{\text{d}t}=-9\text{ cm/s}.\end{aligned}
$$

We would like to find $\frac{\text{d}V}{\text{d}t}$ when $x=40\text{ cm}.$

We start with the formula for the volume of the cube:

$$
V={x}^{3}
$$

Now, we differentiate with respect to time using the chain rule, and we get

$$
\begin{aligned}\frac{\text{d}}{\text{d}t}(V) & =\frac{\text{d}}{\text{d}t}({x}^{3}) \\ \frac{\text{d}V}{\text{d}t} & =3{x}^{2}\frac{\text{d}x}{\text{d}t}.\end{aligned}
$$

We can now plug $x=40$ and $\frac{\text{d}x}{\text{d}t}=-9\text{ cm/s}$ into the expression for $\frac{\text{d}V}{\text{d}t}.$ This gives

$$
\begin{aligned}\frac{\text{d}V}{\text{d}t} & =3{x}^{2}\frac{\text{d}x}{\text{d}t} \\ \frac{\text{d}V}{\text{d}t} & =3(40)^{2}\cdot (-9)\, \\ \frac{\text{d}V}{\text{d}t} & =-43\,200.\end{aligned}
$$

Therefore, the volume of the cube is decreasing at a rate of $43\,200{\text{ cm}}^{3}\text{/s}$ at the moment when $x=40\,\text{cm}.$

A rectangular swimming pool is being drained. If its length and width are $32\text{ m}$ and $12\text{ m}$, respectively, and the water level is falling at a rate of $0.4\,\text{m/min},$ how fast is the water draining out of the pool? Assume that the drain rate is positive and do not round the answer.

The water is draining out at a rate of
{{field-1}}
${\text{m}}^{3}\text{/min}.$
q-314534.worked_solution:
We define the following variables:

- let $L$ and $W$ be the length and width of the swimming pool, respectively, and

- let $h$ and $V$ be the height and volume of the water, respectively.

Note that $h$ and $V$ change with time, while $L$ and $W$ are constants. 

We are given that

$$
L=32\,\text{m},\,W=12\,\text{m},\,\frac{\text{d}h}{\text{d}t}=-0.4\,\text{m}/\text{min}.
$$

We would like to find $\frac{\text{d}V}{\text{d}t}.$

The relation between the two time-dependent variables, $V$ and $h,$ is given by the formula for the volume of water:

$$
V=LWh
$$

We differentiate both sides of $V=LWh$ with respect to $t,$ treating both $L$ and $W$ as constants, and get

$$
\begin{aligned}\frac{\text{d}}{\text{d}t}V & =\frac{\text{d}}{\text{d}t}(LWh) \\ \frac{\text{d}V}{\text{d}t} & =LW\frac{\text{d}h}{\text{d}t}.\end{aligned}
$$

Finally, we can plug in the known values and get

$$
\begin{aligned}\frac{\text{d}V}{\text{d}t} & =(32)(12)\frac{\text{d}h}{\text{d}t} \\ \frac{\text{d}V}{\text{d}t} & =384\cdot (-0.4) \\ \frac{\text{d}V}{\text{d}t} & =-153.6.\end{aligned}
$$

Therefore, the water is draining out at a rate of $153.6\,{\text{m}}^{3}\text{/min}.$

$$

$$

We differentiate both sides of $V=LWh$ with respect to $t,$ treating both $L$ and $W$ as constants, and get

$$

A gas station has a rectangular gasoline storage tank stored underground. The tank is 15 feet long and 10 feet wide. A worker lowers a dip stick into the tank and notices that the depth of the gasoline is decreasing by 2 feet every hour. How fast is the volume of gasoline decreasing?

a
300feet3/hour
b
400feet3/hour
c
440feet3/hour
d
360feet3/hour
e
240feet3/hour
Submit
Correct
EXPLANATION

We define the following variables:

  • let L and W be the length and width of the tank, respectively, and

  • let h and V be the height and volume of the gasoline in the tank, respectively.

Note that h and V change with time, while L and W are constants.

We are given that L=15ft,W=10ft,dhdt=−2ft/hour.

We would like to find dVdt.

The relation between the two time-dependent variables, V and h, is given by the formula for the volume of the gasoline in the tank: V=LWh

We differentiate both sides of V=LWh with respect to t, treating both L and W as constants, and get

ddtV=ddt(LWh)dVdt=LWdhdt.

Finally, we can plug in the known values and get dVdt=(15)(10)dhdtdVdt=150⋅(−2)dVdt=−300.

Therefore, the gasoline level is decreasing at a rate of 300ft3/hour.

John is a carpenter who wants to modify a wooden box. The length, width and height of the box are decreased at a rate of $1\text{ cm/s},$ $2\text{ cm/s}$ and $4\text{ cm/s},$ respectively. Determine the rate at which the volume of the box decreases, if its dimensions are $15\text{ cm}$ long, $10\text{ cm}$ wide and $15\text{ cm}$ high.
q-49012.worked_solution:
Let $L,$ $W,$ $H$ and $V$ be the length, the width, the height, and the volume of the box, respectively. We know that

$$
\begin{aligned}L=15\text{ cm},\, & W=10\text{ cm}, \\ H=15\text{ cm},\, & \frac{\text{d}L}{\text{d}t}=-1\text{ cm/s}, \\ \frac{\text{d}W}{\text{d}t}=-2\text{ cm/s},\, & \frac{\text{d}H}{\text{d}t}=-4\text{ cm/s}.\end{aligned}
$$

We would like to find $\frac{\text{d}V}{\text{d}t}.$

The relation between the four variables is given by the formula for the volume of a rectangular prism:

$$
V=LWH
$$

We differentiate both sides of $V=LWH$ with respect to $t,$ using the product rule, we have

$$
\begin{aligned}\frac{\text{d}}{\text{d}t}V & =\frac{\text{d}}{\text{d}t}(LWH) \\ \frac{\text{d}V}{\text{d}t} & =W\cdot H(\frac{\text{d}L}{\text{d}t})+L\cdot H(\frac{\text{d}W}{\text{d}t})+L\cdot W(\frac{\text{d}H}{\text{d}t}).\end{aligned}
$$

Finally, we can plug in the known values and get

$$
\begin{aligned}\frac{\text{d}V}{\text{d}t} & =(10)(15)(-1)+(15)(15)(-2)+(15)(10)(-4) \\  & =-1\,200{\text{ cm}}^{3}/\text{s}.\end{aligned}
$$

Therefore, the volume of the box is decreasing at a rate of $1\,200{\text{ cm}}^{3}/\text{s}.$
